title: Chapter 144 — Delivery Damage to the Home
intro: Scratched hardwood floors, dinged door frames, cracked tiles — this is no longer about an appliance.

sections.title: Immediate Response
sections.content:
When the delivery crew damages the customer's home, the complaint shifts from appliance territory to home territory. The emotional weight is completely different — this is their house, not a product they can return.

Respond immediately. Do not wait for the customer to call — the delivery crew should report it before they leave. Photos from all angles — taken at the scene, not after the fact. Close-ups and wide shots showing context.

Acknowledge without arguing fault on-site. 'I am documenting this right now and I will file the claim today.' Do NOT say 'our insurance will handle it' — that sounds like you are passing responsibility to a faceless company. Say 'I am taking care of this personally.'

Give the customer your direct contact info — not a general line, not a claims department number. Your name, your number. They need to know a human being is responsible for making this right.

sections.title: The Repair Coordination
sections.content:
File the damage claim with your delivery company's insurance the same day. Get a repair estimate from a qualified contractor within 48 hours — not a week, 48 hours. Keep the customer informed at every step.

The math is simple: covering repair costs without argument is almost always cheaper than losing the customer, the Google review, the referrals, and the reputation damage. A $300 floor repair versus a $30,000 lifetime customer value — that is not even a decision.

If the insurance process is slow, consider fronting the repair cost and recovering from insurance later. The customer should not wait for your insurance company's timeline. They should experience your timeline — which is fast, responsive, and human.

sections.title: Prevention
sections.content:
Floor runners on every delivery — from the truck to the installation location. Door protectors on every doorway the appliance passes through. Crew training on navigating tight spaces — measure the path before moving the appliance, not while moving it.

Pre-delivery path assessment for premium deliveries — built-in refrigeration, pro-style ranges, anything over 300 pounds. Walk the path virtually with the customer during the pre-delivery call: 'How wide is your front door? Any stairs? Any tight turns?'

One incident per 100 deliveries is industry average. Reducing it to one per 200 through prevention saves thousands per year in claims and immeasurably more in customer trust. Prevention is cheaper than repair in every single case.
